title: International Perspectives on Inclusion and Exclusion
text:
Who belongs, who takes part, and on whose terms? In the seminar International Perspectives on Inclusion and Exclusion, we look at how societies draw these boundaries in schools, labour markets, citizenship law and social services, and how they do so differently from country to country.
This script accompanies the seminar. Here you will not only read: you will match, classify and recall. Take your time, try things out, and come back whenever you like.


The script is organised in seven parts, followed by a practice section. You can reach all pages through the menu on the left.



Part I · Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
Chapter 1 introduces the topic, its history and the key terms, and discusses the dimensions, dynamics and normative foundations of inclusion and exclusion.



Parts II–VII · From theory to practice
Central theories; power, difference and inequality; institutions; international comparison; inclusion as a political task; research and critical debates.



Practice · Learning Games
A memory game and eight international cases to classify. About 20 minutes.



Practice · Learning Check
A short test of what you have retained.

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
text: Inclusion and exclusion are not characteristics of individuals. Nobody is “excluded” in the way they are tall or short. The terms describe relations: between people and groups, between people and institutions, and between those who draw boundaries and those who are affected by them.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
text:
No inside without an outside
Every inclusion implies a boundary. A community, a nation or an organisation defines who belongs. In doing so, it also defines who does not belong. Citizenship is a clear example. It grants rights to members and, at the same time, distinguishes them from non-citizens. Inclusion and exclusion are therefore two sides of the same process, not opposites that exclude each other.
This has an important consequence. Whoever asks why some people are excluded must also ask who includes, on what terms and in whose interest.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
text:
Boundaries are made
The established–outsider study by Norbert Elias and John Scotson illustrates this. In an English suburb, an older group of residents looked down on newcomers, although both groups had similar jobs and incomes. The only difference was the length of residence. The established group used gossip, cohesion and control over local institutions to keep the newcomers in an inferior position. The boundary did not result from differences between the groups. It produced them.
Similar processes can be observed today: in debates on “real” members of a nation, in the distinction between “us” and “migrants” in the third generation, or in neighbourhoods that are labelled as problem areas.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
section: Inclusion depends on the reference point
text:
Inclusion depends on the reference point
Whether someone counts as included depends on the reference point. A person can be well integrated into family and community networks but excluded from the labour market. A refugee can attend a language course but have no right to work. A pupil can attend a mainstream school but sit in a separate group most of the day. One should therefore always ask: included in what, and excluded from what?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts
text:
Consequences for analysis and practice
A relational view avoids two shortcuts. The first locates the causes of exclusion solely in the deficits of individuals. The second treats people as passive victims of structures. Both overlook that boundaries are negotiated and contested, and that people respond to them.
For social work practice, this means: look at the relations, not only at the “case”. Ask who holds the power to define boundaries and what scope for action the people concerned have.






NoteReflection question



Choose a group that is often described as “excluded”. Who draws the boundary in this case, and which institutions are involved?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.5 Inclusion and exclusion as relational concepts

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text: Inclusion is usually seen as the positive counterpart to exclusion. This view is too simple. Inclusive measures can themselves produce new boundaries. Recognising this ambivalence is not an argument against inclusion. It is a condition for implementing it well.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
Inclusion on whose terms?
Being included often means adapting to existing norms. Integration policies may expect migrants to give up parts of their identity. Labour market programmes may define participation exclusively as paid work and devalue care work or voluntary engagement. Those who do not fit the norm remain at the margin, now as “failures of integration”. Inclusion on unequal terms can thus stabilise hierarchies.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
The dilemma of difference
To receive support, people often have to be classified: as having special educational needs, as disabled, as refugees, as “at risk”. The classification opens access to resources. At the same time, it can stigmatise and separate. Martha Minow called this the dilemma of difference: ignoring difference can perpetuate disadvantage, but highlighting difference can do so as well. In German-speaking debates, the term Etikettierungs-Ressourcen-Dilemma (labelling–resources dilemma) describes the same tension in schools.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
Differential inclusion
Many people are neither fully included nor fully excluded. Migration research speaks of differential inclusion: migrants are included in the labour market, for example, but with fewer rights, in insecure positions and under constant threat of exclusion. Their inclusion is real, but it is subordinate. The boundary does not run between inside and outside. It runs through the inside.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
Inclusion that excludes others
Inclusion of one group can also come at the expense of another. Welfare states that strengthen solidarity among citizens may tighten access for non-citizens. Communities that grow closer may draw sharper boundaries against outsiders. Social cohesion can turn into closure.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?
text:
Consequences
These ambivalences call for a critical but not cynical stance. The question is not whether inclusion is good, but how it is designed: who defines its terms, who participates in decisions, and which new boundaries emerge.
For social work practice, this means reflecting on one’s own categories and procedures. Professionals should ask regularly: whom do our offers reach, whom do they miss, and which labels do we attach to people in order to help them?






NoteReflection question



Find an example of an inclusive measure that has unintended exclusionary effects. How could the measure be redesigned?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.8 The ambivalence of inclusion: Can inclusion also produce exclusion?

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text: Exclusion can result from the actions of individuals, from the rules and routines of institutions and from the structures of a society. These three levels are analytically distinct. In practice they overlap and reinforce each other.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text:
The individual level
At the individual level, exclusion occurs in interactions: a landlord who does not rent to people with a certain name, a teacher who has lower expectations of some pupils, a remark in a meeting that marks a colleague as “other”. Prejudice, stereotypes and stigma shape such interactions. They are important, but they explain only part of the picture.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text:
The institutional level
Institutions can exclude even if no individual intends to do so. Mechtild Gomolla and Frank-Olaf Radtke showed for German schools that decisions about school entry, special education referrals and secondary school recommendations systematically disadvantage children with a migration background. The reason lies not primarily in individual prejudice, but in organisational routines, criteria and the pressure to produce manageable groups.
Typical mechanisms of institutional exclusion are:

formal requirements that some groups cannot meet, such as documents, language levels or fixed addresses
eligibility rules that tie access to residence status or previous contributions
standard procedures that ignore different needs
the use of categories that become labels
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text:
The structural level
Structural exclusion refers to the distribution of resources and power in society as a whole: in the labour market, the housing market, the education system and the political system. Charles Tilly described how durable inequality arises when categorical differences, such as citizen/non-citizen or man/woman, are linked to unequal access to resources. Exclusion is then reproduced across generations without anyone having to act intentionally.
Racism, sexism and ableism are not only attitudes. They are also inscribed in laws, institutions and social structures.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion

title: 1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion
text:
How the levels interact
The three levels interact. Structural conditions shape institutional rules. Institutional rules give individual prejudices room to operate. Individual actions in turn confirm and stabilise structures. A housing market with little affordable housing creates competition; landlords can choose; discrimination becomes easier and harder to prove.
For social work practice, this means that individual support is necessary but not sufficient. Professionals also need to address institutional routines and, where possible, structural conditions, for example through advocacy, networking and political participation.






NoteReflection question



Choose an organisation you know, such as a school, an agency or an association. Which rules or routines could exclude certain groups, even if no one intends to do so?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.6 Individual, institutional and structural dimensions of inclusion and exclusion

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text: The boundaries of inclusion and exclusion are shifting. Four developments are particularly important: globalisation, migration, digitalisation and broader social transformation. Each of them creates new opportunities for participation and new forms of exclusion.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text:
Globalisation
Global markets connect societies more closely. Production, capital and information move across borders. At the same time, the gains are unevenly distributed. Some regions and groups benefit, while others lose jobs and security. National welfare states have less room to manoeuvre. Exclusion can thus have causes far beyond the local level, and local social work encounters its consequences.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text:
Migration
Migration is a normal feature of modern societies. It raises the question of who belongs and under what conditions. Residence status, citizenship rules and asylum procedures create graded forms of membership, from full citizens to people with temporary protection or without papers. Debates on migration often serve to draw symbolic boundaries between “us” and “them”. At the same time, migrants and their descendants claim participation and change societies from within.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text:
Digitalisation
Digital technologies open new forms of access to information, education, services and political participation. They also create new divides. Research distinguishes several levels of the digital divide: access to devices and internet, skills to use them, and the benefits people can actually derive from them. As public services move online, those without access or skills risk being cut off. Algorithmic systems in recruitment, credit scoring or social administration can reproduce discrimination, often in ways that are difficult to see and to contest.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
text:
Social transformation
Further developments reshape inclusion and exclusion: climate change and its unequal consequences, demographic ageing, changes in work and employment, growing inequality and political polarisation. Several crises overlap and reinforce each other. They put pressure on welfare systems and can increase competition for resources. In such situations, the willingness to include others may decline, and exclusionary rhetoric can gain support.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation

title: 1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation
section: What this means for the seminar
text:
What this means for the seminar
These developments show why the topic remains relevant. Inclusion and exclusion are not settled questions. They are renegotiated under changing conditions.
For social work practice, this means keeping both levels in view: supporting people in concrete situations and analysing the broader transformations that shape their lives. The following parts of the seminar take up these challenges in an international comparison.






NoteReflection question



Which of the four developments affects the addressees of social work in your region most strongly? Give a concrete example.

1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.10 Contemporary challenges: Globalization, migration, digitalization and social transformation

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text: The terms inclusion and exclusion are relatively young in public debate. The phenomena they describe are old. Every society has drawn boundaries between members and strangers, between the “deserving” and the “undeserving” poor, between those with rights and those without.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.3 Historical development of the concepts

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text:
Early roots in sociology
Classical sociology already dealt with belonging and its limits. Max Weber described social closure: groups secure advantages by restricting access to insiders. Georg Simmel analysed the figure of the stranger, who is part of a group and yet remains outside. Norbert Elias and John Scotson showed in their study The Established and the Outsiders (1965) how an established group stigmatises newcomers, although the two groups hardly differ socially.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.3 Historical development of the concepts

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text:
Exclusion in French social policy
The modern career of the term “exclusion” began in France. In 1974, René Lenoir published Les exclus, a book about people who had fallen through the net of social protection, among them people with disabilities, older people and young people without work. In the 1980s and 1990s, the term spread in French debates on long-term unemployment and the crisis of the suburbs. Robert Castel spoke of désaffiliation: the gradual loss of ties to work and social networks.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.3 Historical development of the concepts

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text:
European and international policy
From the late 1980s, the European Community and later the European Union adopted the language of social exclusion. It allowed poverty to be described as more than a lack of income. Since then, EU indicators have measured the risk of “poverty or social exclusion”. International organisations took up the concept as well.
In parallel, sociologists developed different readings of exclusion. Hilary Silver (1994) distinguished three paradigms: exclusion as a breakdown of social solidarity, as a result of specialisation and individual choice, and as an outcome of group monopolies. Ruth Levitas (1998) showed that political discourses use the term in different ways: to argue for redistribution, to emphasise integration into paid work, or to blame an allegedly deviant “underclass”.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.3 Historical development of the concepts

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
section: Inclusion in education and disability rights
text:
Inclusion in education and disability rights
The term inclusion has a second, partly separate origin in education and the disability rights movement. The UNESCO Salamanca Statement (1994) called for schools that welcome all children. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006) made inclusion a binding human right. Here, inclusion stands for a change of systems rather than for the adaptation of individuals.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.3 Historical development of the concepts

title: 1.3 Historical development of the concepts
text:
Systems theory
In German-speaking sociology, Niklas Luhmann used inclusion and exclusion in a different sense. For him, inclusion means that persons are taken into account by function systems such as the economy, law or education. Exclusion in one system can trigger exclusion in others.
The concepts thus have several histories. Knowing these histories helps to understand why the same words carry different meanings today.






NoteReflection question



Compare the French debate on exclusion with the disability rights debate on inclusion. What problem does each of them address, and what solution do they suggest?
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.3 Historical development of the concepts

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text: Exclusion is rarely a single event. It usually develops over time and across several areas of life. Inclusion, too, is not a state that is achieved once and for all. Both are processes.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text:
Exclusion as a process
Robert Castel described exclusion as a gradual movement from a zone of integration through a zone of vulnerability into a zone of désaffiliation. A person loses a stable job, takes up precarious work, falls into debt, loses the flat, and contacts thin out. Each step makes the next one more likely. Seen this way, exclusion is not a fixed position at the margin, but the result of a trajectory.
This perspective has practical value. It shows that there are points at which a downward process can be interrupted, and that prevention is possible.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text:
Multiple dimensions
Exclusion has several dimensions that reinforce each other:

economic: income, work, housing
social: networks, contacts, support
political and legal: rights, residence status, participation
cultural and symbolic: recognition, stigma, representation

A person can be included in one dimension and excluded in another. Problems tend to accumulate, however. Poverty restricts social contacts; an insecure residence status blocks access to work; stigma makes it harder to claim rights. Research therefore speaks of cumulative disadvantage.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text:
Intersectionality
Dimensions of difference also overlap. Gender, race, class, disability, age and residence status do not simply add up. They interact and produce specific positions. An older woman with a refugee background experiences different barriers than a young man with the same background. Intersectional analysis helps to recognise such positions and to avoid one-dimensional explanations.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: 1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes
text:
Inclusion is never finished
Inclusion processes can be reversed. Rights that were granted can be restricted. Reforms can be implemented half-heartedly. Groups that were once accepted can become targets of new exclusion, for example in times of crisis or political polarisation. Inclusion therefore requires constant attention and is always contested.
For social work practice, this means that biographies and life courses matter. Professionals need to understand how disadvantages have built up over time, and where there are points for intervention.






NoteReflection question



Describe a possible path into exclusion for a fictional person. At which points could social work have intervened?

1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.7 Inclusion and exclusion as dynamic and multidimensional processes

title: Inclusion and Exclusion: Theories and Concepts
text:
This page introduces the theories that guide the seminar. They answer different questions. Social exclusion theory and welfare regimes explain how institutions regulate access. Bourdieu shows why formally equal chances are used unequally. Intersectionality and citizenship ask who counts as belonging at all. Postcolonial perspectives widen the view to global and historical hierarchies. The capability approach and human rights provide a normative standard for social work.
Each theory follows the same structure: a short summary, its key claims, its main representatives and the criticism it has received. The criticism answers a question from the Comparison Grid: What does our theory explain – and what not?

title: Inclusion and Exclusion: Theories and Concepts
text:
Phase I: Understanding
How do societies organise inclusion and exclusion?

Social exclusion
Session 1 · Can someone be included and excluded at the same time?
Summary. Social exclusion theory describes exclusion as a process, not as a fixed state. People can be cut off from income, work, rights, social relations and political participation, and these dimensions tend to reinforce each other. Hilary Silver showed that the idea of an inclusive society itself differs between countries: what counts as exclusion depends on what a society regards as the basis of belonging. Systems theory adds a second perspective: a person can be included in one social system and excluded from another at the same time.
Key claims

Exclusion is multidimensional: economic, social, political and cultural dimensions interact.
Exclusion is relational: it results from the actions of institutions and other groups, not only from individual deficits.
National traditions frame exclusion differently. Silver distinguishes three paradigms: solidarity (exclusion as a breakdown of the social bond, typical of French republicanism), specialisation (exclusion as discrimination and blocked exchange, typical of liberal traditions) and monopoly (exclusion as the result of group closure and privilege).
In systems theory (Luhmann), modern societies include people through function systems such as the economy, law, education and health. Exclusion from one system often leads to exclusion from others.

Representatives

Hilary Silver: Social exclusion and social solidarity: Three paradigms (1994); The contexts of social inclusion (2015)
Robert Castel: Les métamorphoses de la question sociale (1995)
Ruth Levitas: The Inclusive Society? Social Exclusion and New Labour (1998)
Niklas Luhmann: systems-theoretical concept of inclusion and exclusion (short input only)

Criticism

The concept is vague and can be stretched to cover almost any disadvantage, which weakens its analytical value.
Policies often reduce inclusion to labour market participation; Levitas showed how this shifts attention from inequality to the individual’s employability.
The image of “inside” and “outside” hides that most exclusion happens within society: people are rarely fully outside, but at its precarious margins.
The debate emerged in France and the European Union and does not easily fit societies with large informal sectors.



Welfare regimes
Session 2 · How do welfare systems decide who gets support?
Summary. Gøsta Esping-Andersen compared welfare states in Western democracies and identified three regime types. They differ in how far they protect people from market dependence, how they stratify society and how they divide responsibility between state, market and family. The typology helps to explain why the same social risk – unemployment, illness, single parenthood – leads to very different outcomes in different countries.
Key claims

Decommodification is a central criterion: the degree to which people can maintain their living standard without depending on the labour market.
The liberal regime (for example the USA, the UK) relies on the market and means-tested benefits; the conservative-corporatist regime (for example Germany) ties benefits to employment and status and relies on the family; the social democratic regime (for example Sweden) offers universal benefits based on citizenship or residence.
Welfare states do not only reduce inequality; they also create and stabilise their own hierarchies between groups.
Access to protection always has boundaries: those who do not fit the regime’s logic, such as people without stable employment or legal status, fall through the net.

Representatives

Gøsta Esping-Andersen: The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism (1990)
Wil Arts and John Gelissen: Three worlds of welfare capitalism or more? (2002), an overview of the debate
Ian Gough: Globalization and regional welfare regimes: The East Asian case (2001)

Criticism

Feminist scholars such as Jane Lewis (1992) and Ann Orloff (1993) criticised that the typology neglects gender, unpaid care work and the male-breadwinner model.
The three types hardly fit welfare arrangements outside Europe and North America; researchers have proposed further regimes, for example for Southern Europe, East Asia and Latin America.
Most countries are hybrids, and welfare states change over time, so fixed types can obscure reforms.
The typology focuses on citizens and workers and says little about migrants’ unequal access to social rights.



Forms of capital and habitus
Session 3 · Why do equal rules produce unequal results?
Summary. Pierre Bourdieu explains why formally equal opportunities do not lead to equal outcomes. People bring different amounts of economic, cultural and social capital into institutions such as schools. These institutions treat the habitus of privileged groups as natural talent and reward it. Inequality is thus reproduced through seemingly neutral procedures.
Key claims

Economic capital (money, property), cultural capital (knowledge, education, taste, credentials) and social capital (networks and relationships) can be converted into each other.
Cultural capital exists in embodied form (dispositions, language), objectified form (books, instruments) and institutionalised form (degrees and certificates).
Habitus is a system of durable dispositions shaped by one’s social position; it guides perception and action largely without conscious reflection.
The education system legitimises social inequality by turning social background into apparently individual achievement.

Representatives

Pierre Bourdieu: The forms of capital (1986); Distinction (French 1979, English 1984)
Pierre Bourdieu and Jean-Claude Passeron: Reproduction in Education, Society and Culture (French 1970, English 1977)

Criticism

The concept of habitus is often read as deterministic; it leaves little room for agency, upward mobility and social change.
The theory was developed in the French context; what counts as legitimate culture differs between societies (Lamont and Lareau 1988).
Gender, ethnicity and racism play only a secondary role in Bourdieu’s work.
The concepts are hard to measure; empirical studies often reduce cultural capital to visits to museums or the number of books at home.
crumbs: Theories and Concepts

title: Inclusion and Exclusion: Theories and Concepts
section: Phase II: Comparing power and belonging
text:
Phase II: Comparing power and belonging
Why are some groups excluded – and how differently does this happen across contexts?

Intersectionality and Critical Race Theory
Session 4 · How do race, gender and class work together?
Summary. Intersectionality shows that discrimination cannot be understood as the sum of separate characteristics. Kimberlé Crenshaw developed the term from legal cases in which Black women were not protected, because courts examined either racial or sex discrimination, but not both together. Critical Race Theory (CRT) adds that racism is not an exception in otherwise neutral institutions but part of their everyday functioning.
Key claims

Categories such as race, gender, class and disability interact and produce specific experiences of disadvantage and privilege.
Power relations operate on several levels at once: structural, institutional, interpersonal and in representations.
CRT holds that racism is ordinary and structural; formally colour-blind rules can reproduce racial inequality.
The perspectives and experiences of those affected are a source of knowledge (in CRT, for example, through counter-storytelling).

Representatives

Kimberlé Crenshaw: Demarginalizing the intersection of race and sex (1989); Mapping the margins (1991)
Patricia Hill Collins: Black Feminist Thought (1990); with Sirma Bilge: Intersectionality (2nd ed. 2020)
Derrick Bell, Richard Delgado and Jean Stefancic as founding figures of Critical Race Theory

Criticism

It remains unclear which and how many categories an analysis must include, and how they can be studied empirically (McCall 2005).
The approach risks fixing people in identity categories instead of analysing the processes that produce them.
Concepts from the US cannot be transferred directly to contexts such as Germany, where the term “race” is avoided and racism is often discussed under other headings.
In public debate, both approaches are strongly politicised, which makes careful use in teaching and practice more demanding.



Citizenship
Session 5 · Who belongs – and who has access to rights?
Summary. Citizenship defines who is a full member of a political community and who has which rights. T. H. Marshall described the historical development of citizenship in England as an expansion from civil to political and finally to social rights. Later research broadened the concept: citizenship includes legal status, rights, participation and a sense of belonging, and these dimensions do not always coincide.
Key claims

Marshall distinguishes civil rights (freedom, property, justice), political rights (voting, standing for office) and social rights (education, social security, a decent standard of living).
Citizenship creates equality of status that can limit the effects of class inequality.
Bloemraad, Korteweg and Yurdakul distinguish four dimensions: legal status, rights, participation and belonging.
Formal rights do not guarantee real access: people can hold citizenship and still be treated as outsiders, and non-citizens can hold some rights through residence or human rights.

Representatives

T. H. Marshall: Citizenship and Social Class (1950)
Rogers Brubaker: Citizenship and Nationhood in France and Germany (1992)
Yasemin Soysal: Limits of Citizenship (1994), on postnational membership
Irene Bloemraad, Anna Korteweg and Gökçe Yurdakul: Citizenship and immigration (2008)

Criticism

Marshall’s model is based on the English case and assumes a linear progress of rights that does not apply to many countries.
It largely ignores women, migrants and colonial subjects, who received rights later, partially or not at all.
Rights can be restricted again, as debates on social benefits for migrants show.
Approaches that stress postnational rights tend to underestimate how strongly the nation state still decides on residence, work and social protection.



Social model of disability
Session 6 · Is equal access the same as real participation?
Summary. The social model distinguishes between impairment, a physical, sensory or mental condition, and disability, the disadvantage that society produces through barriers and exclusion. It was developed by disabled activists in Britain and moved the focus from the individual body to social structures. The model shaped the disability rights movement and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).
Key claims

People are disabled by barriers in buildings, communication, institutions and attitudes, not by their impairment as such.
The medical model treats disability as an individual problem to be cured or compensated; the social model treats it as a matter of rights and social change.
Removing barriers is a collective responsibility, not a favour to individuals.
Disabled people are experts on their own lives: “nothing about us without us”.

Representatives

Union of the Physically Impaired Against Segregation (UPIAS): Fundamental Principles of Disability (1976)
Michael Oliver: The Politics of Disablement (1990)
Colin Barnes: Disabled People in Britain and Discrimination (1991)
Tom Shakespeare: The social model of disability (2017) – a short presentation of the model that also names its limits

Criticism

The strict separation of impairment and disability neglects the experience of the body, pain and illness; this critique came, among others, from feminist disability scholars and from Shakespeare.
A world entirely free of barriers is not achievable, because different impairments can require contradictory adjustments.
The model emerged in Britain; in contexts with widespread poverty and weak public services, impairment and poverty are closely intertwined.
The model explains what disables people but says less about how much real freedom they have, a gap that the capability approach addresses.



Capability approach
Session 6 · What can people actually do and be?
Summary. The capability approach judges well-being and justice not by income or resources, but by people’s real freedoms to live a life they have reason to value. Amartya Sen developed it as an alternative to purely economic measures of development; Martha Nussbaum extended it into a theory of justice. For inclusion research, it shows why the same resources lead to different opportunities.
Key claims

Functionings are what a person actually does or is, for example being educated, healthy or employed; capabilities are the real options a person has to achieve such functionings.
Conversion factors determine how far resources can be turned into capabilities: personal factors (for example an impairment), social factors (for example norms or discrimination) and environmental factors (for example infrastructure).
Agency matters: people should be able to choose between options, not merely receive outcomes.
Nussbaum proposes a list of central capabilities that every just society should secure at a threshold level.

Representatives

Amartya Sen: Commodities and Capabilities (1985); Development as Freedom (1999)
Martha Nussbaum: Women and Human Development (2000); Creating Capabilities (2011)
Sophie Mitra: The capability approach and disability (2006)

Criticism

The approach is difficult to operationalise; it remains open which capabilities to measure and how.
Sen refuses a fixed list of capabilities, while Nussbaum’s universal list is criticised as paternalistic and culturally biased.
The focus on individual freedoms can neglect power relations, collective action and the structures that produce exclusion.
As a normative framework, it says what should be achieved but offers little explanation of why exclusion arises.



Postcolonial and decolonial perspectives
Session 7 · Why can’t we understand exclusion only within one country?
Summary. Postcolonial and decolonial perspectives argue that present-day exclusion cannot be understood without colonial history and global power relations. They criticise how the “West” has represented other societies and how knowledge, including knowledge in social work, still flows mainly from the Global North to the Global South. The seminar distinguishes three lenses: postcolonial theory, decolonial theory and world-systems analysis.
Key claims

Postcolonial theory (Said) analyses how colonial discourses constructed “the Orient” or “the Other” as different and inferior, and how such representations continue today.
Decolonial theory (Quijano) describes a coloniality of power: racial classification, the global division of labour and Eurocentric knowledge outlasted formal colonialism.
World-systems analysis (Wallerstein) explains global inequality through a capitalist world economy divided into core, semi-periphery and periphery.
International social work has often exported Western models; decolonising social work means questioning its own theories, methods and standards (Razack).

Representatives

Edward Said: Orientalism (1978)
Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak: Can the subaltern speak? (1988)
Immanuel Wallerstein: The Modern World-System (vol. 1, 1974)
Aníbal Quijano: Coloniality of power, Eurocentrism, and Latin America (2000)
Raewyn Connell: Southern Theory (2007)
Narda Razack: Decolonizing the pedagogy and practice of international social work (2009)

Criticism

Postcolonial theory has been criticised for focusing on discourse and representation while neglecting economic structures and class (for example by Vivek Chibber, 2013).
World-systems analysis, in turn, is criticised as economistic; it pays little attention to culture, agency and differences within regions.
Talking about “the West” and “the Global South” risks homogenising very different societies.
The approaches are often abstract and hard to translate into concrete analysis or practice.

title: Inclusion and Exclusion: Theories and Concepts
text:
Phase III: Acting and reflecting
What can social work do without reproducing exclusion?

Social work as a human rights profession
Session 8 · Does social work include – or control?
Summary. Social work does not stand outside the structures it analyses: it can open up participation and at the same time control, normalise and exclude. In the German debate, the double mandate describes the tension between help for clients and control on behalf of the state and society. Silvia Staub-Bernasconi added a third mandate based on professional knowledge, ethics and human rights. Internationally, the global definition of social work names human rights and social justice as central principles.
Key claims

Social workers act between the interests of their clients and the expectations of the state and their employers.
Human rights offer a normative standard that goes beyond national law and allows social workers to criticise exclusionary rules.
Social work has a mandate not only for individual help but also for structural change on the meso and macro levels.
Historically, the profession has been closely linked to human rights internationally, but it has also taken part in exclusionary practices.

Representatives

Lothar Böhnisch and Hans Lösch: concept of the double mandate (1973)
Silvia Staub-Bernasconi: Soziale Arbeit als Handlungswissenschaft (2007), on the triple mandate
Jim Ife: Human Rights and Social Work (3rd ed. 2012)
Lynne Healy: Exploring the history of social work as a human rights profession (2008)
IFSW and IASSW: Global Definition of Social Work (2014)

Criticism

Universal human rights are criticised as Western; their application in other cultural contexts is contested.
The third mandate is self-given by the profession; critics ask how it can be legitimised against democratically decided law.
There is a gap between the human rights rhetoric of the profession and practice, for example where social workers are involved in implementing asylum or benefit sanctions.
Where social work is mainly financed by humanitarian organisations, as in Lebanon, the double mandate takes a different form, so the concept cannot be transferred unchanged.

title: Inclusion and Exclusion: Learning Games
text:
Who belongs, who takes part, and on whose terms? The seminar International Perspectives on Inclusion and Exclusion examines how societies draw and shift these boundaries: in schools and labour markets, in citizenship law, in social services and in everyday interaction. Comparing different countries shows that the same terms can describe very different practices, and that seemingly inclusive measures can still keep people apart.
Precise terms are the basis for this comparison. Exclusion, segregation, integration and inclusion are often used interchangeably in public debate, although they describe different relationships between people and institutions. A particularly common assumption is that integration already amounts to inclusion: anyone who is inside the system is considered included.
The two learning games on this page help you to work with these distinctions. The memory game lets you recall ten key terms and their definitions. In the second game, you apply the four central terms to eight international cases and explain your choice. Plan about 20 minutes for both games.

title: 1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies
text: Modern societies promise equal participation. Constitutions, human rights treaties and welfare states formulate the claim that every person should have access to education, work, health care and political participation. At the same time, inequality persists, and in some areas it grows. The tension between the promise of inclusion and the reality of exclusion is a defining feature of contemporary societies.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies

title: 1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies
section: From “above and below” to “inside and outside”
text:
From “above and below” to “inside and outside”
For a long time, social inequality was mainly described in terms of class and stratification: who is above and who is below. Since the 1980s, a second image has gained ground: who is inside and who is outside. Long-term unemployment, precarious work, the concentration of poverty in certain neighbourhoods and the exclusion of migrants from rights made it clear that some people are not simply lower in the hierarchy. They risk losing their connection to central areas of society altogether.
The two images do not replace each other. Inequality and exclusion are linked. But the language of inclusion and exclusion directs attention to thresholds, boundaries and processes of detachment.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies

title: 1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies
section: Areas where the boundaries become visible
text:
Areas where the boundaries become visible
Inclusion and exclusion matter in almost every area of life:

Education: access to schools, segregated school systems, educational qualifications as gateways
Labour market: unemployment, precarious employment, recognition of foreign qualifications
Citizenship and residence: voting rights, access to social benefits, deportation
Health and care: access to services, barriers for people without insurance or without a secure status
Housing and urban space: segregation, displacement, homelessness
Political participation and public discourse: whose voice is heard and whose is not

1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies

title: 1.2 The significance of inclusion and exclusion in contemporary societies
section: Inclusion as a political and normative goal
text:
Inclusion as a political and normative goal
Inclusion has also become a political programme. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities establishes inclusion as a human rights obligation. The European Union has made the fight against poverty and social exclusion a policy goal. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development commits states to “leave no one behind”.
Such commitments are important. They create a reference point for claims and for criticism. Yet they also raise questions. Who defines what full participation means? Which forms of difference are recognised, and which are expected to disappear? These questions run through the whole seminar.






NoteReflection question



In which of the areas listed above do you see the strongest boundaries in your own country? What evidence would you need to support your assessment?

title: 1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance
text:
A young woman with a migration history finishes school with good grades but receives no invitations to job interviews. A wheelchair user can enrol at a university, but the seminar room is on the second floor of a building without a lift. A family lives in a city for twenty years without the right to vote in national elections. All three are formally part of society. Yet each of them experiences a boundary: between those who belong fully and those who belong only partly, conditionally or not at all.
These scenes condense the subject of this seminar. Inclusion and exclusion describe how societies draw and shift such boundaries. They concern access to rights, resources and recognition, and they concern the question of who defines the rules of access.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance

title: 1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance
text:
Why the topic matters
The terms have become key words of public debate. They appear in education policy, in disability rights, in migration and integration policy, in poverty reports and in the programmes of international organisations. Their popularity has a downside. The more often they are used, the less clear their meaning becomes. “Inclusion” can mean a human right, a school reform or simply a friendly gesture. “Exclusion” can describe extreme poverty, but also a lack of contacts or a missing passport.
This seminar therefore asks for precision. It treats inclusion and exclusion not as slogans, but as analytical concepts. They help to describe social positions, to identify mechanisms and to evaluate institutions.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance

title: 1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance
text:
Relevance for social work
Social work operates at the boundaries of inclusion and exclusion. Its addressees are often people whose participation is restricted: through poverty, disability, residence status, racism or age. At the same time, social work is itself part of the institutions that grant or deny access. It decides about eligibility, assigns support and categorises cases.
For professional practice, this means a double task. Social workers support people in gaining access. And they reflect critically on how their own organisations include and exclude.

title: 1.1 Introduction to the topic and its relevance
text:
Why an international perspective?
Comparing countries shows that the same terms describe very different practices. A school system that calls itself inclusive in one country may still separate children in another sense. Citizenship rules, welfare regimes and anti-discrimination laws vary widely. The comparison sharpens the view of one’s own society. What appears natural at home turns out to be one option among several.






NoteReflection question



Think of a situation from your everyday life or a placement in which a person was formally included but did not really belong. What made the difference?

text: Who belongs, who takes part, and who decides? This first chapter lays the groundwork for the seminar. It introduces the topic, traces how the concepts developed and clarifies the key terms. It then shows that inclusion and exclusion are relational, multidimensional and dynamic, and that inclusion itself can be ambivalent. The chapter closes with the normative foundations of the debate and with the challenges that currently reshape it.

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text: Talking about inclusion and exclusion is never purely descriptive. Whoever calls a situation “exclusion” implies that something is wrong. The debate therefore rests on normative foundations. Four of them are central: equality, freedom, justice and human dignity.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Human dignity
Human dignity is the starting point. Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. The German Basic Law opens with the principle that human dignity shall be inviolable. Dignity does not depend on achievement, origin or usefulness. It is the reason why exclusion from basic rights cannot be justified by such criteria.
crumbs: Part I – Foundations and Theoretical Approaches
1. Introduction: Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion
1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Equality
Equality has several meanings. Formal equality means equal rights and equal treatment before the law. Substantive equality asks whether people actually have equal opportunities. Equal treatment can produce unequal outcomes if starting conditions differ. This is why the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities requires reasonable accommodation, and why anti-discrimination law also covers indirect discrimination.

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Freedom
Freedom is often understood negatively, as protection from interference. Exclusion, however, also restricts freedom in a positive sense: the real possibility to shape one’s own life. Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum developed the capability approach to capture this. What counts is not only which resources people have, but what they can actually do and be with them.

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Justice
Theories of justice offer different answers to the question of what a just society owes its members. John Rawls focused on the fair distribution of basic goods. Nancy Fraser argued that justice requires redistribution, recognition and representation, so that everyone can participate as a peer in social life. Axel Honneth emphasised that misrecognition, such as disrespect and humiliation, is an injustice in its own right.

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
text:
Tensions between the principles
The principles do not always point in the same direction. Equal treatment can conflict with the recognition of difference. Freedom of association can conflict with non-discrimination. Such tensions cannot be resolved once and for all. They must be weighed in each context.

title: 1.9 Normative foundations: Equality, freedom, justice and human dignity
section: Social work as a human rights profession
text:
Social work as a human rights profession
The global definition of social work by the International Federation of Social Workers (IFSW) names social justice, human rights, collective responsibility and respect for diversities as central principles. For social work practice, this means that the normative foundations are not abstract. They are a professional mandate: to make exclusion visible, to justify interventions and to take a position where rights are violated.






NoteReflection question



Take a concrete case of exclusion. Which principle (equality, freedom, justice, dignity) is violated most clearly, and why?

title: 1.4 Key terms and conceptual distinctions
text:
Exclusion, segregation, integration and inclusion


Social exclusion

Social exclusion describes a process in which people are cut off from rights, resources and participation in the mainstream life of a society. It is multidimensional: disadvantages in income, work, housing, health, education and social contacts tend to reinforce each other. The term directs attention to the institutions and mechanisms that exclude, not only to the situation of those affected.

Often confused with: poverty. Poverty usually refers to a lack of income at a given point in time, whereas social exclusion is a process that spans several areas of life.




Segregation

Segregation means that groups are separated physically or institutionally into distinct spaces, schools or services. Those affected are inside the system, for example they attend school, but in separate institutions. Segregation can be required by law or emerge from housing markets, school choice and administrative practice.

Often confused with: exclusion. Segregated groups are not cut off from a system; they are kept apart within it.




Integration

Integration refers to incorporating individuals or groups into existing structures, such as mainstream schools or the labour market. The structures themselves largely remain unchanged, and those who are integrated are expected to adapt. In migration debates, the term covers very different meanings, ranging from equal participation to cultural adaptation.

Often confused with: inclusion, or blurred with assimilation, the demand to give up one’s own cultural identity.




Inclusion

Inclusion means changing structures so that everyone can participate fully and on equal terms. The system adapts to the diversity of people, not the other way round. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) establishes inclusive education as a right.

Often confused with: integration. Placing someone in a mainstream setting is not yet inclusion if teaching, rules and materials stay the same.

title: 1.4 Key terms and conceptual distinctions
text:
Mechanisms of exclusion


Marginalisation

Marginalisation describes how groups are pushed to the edges of power, resources and participation while formally remaining members of society. Marginalised groups have rights on paper but little influence on the decisions that affect them. The term captures positions between full participation and exclusion.

Often confused with: full exclusion, or with minority status, which refers to numbers rather than to power.




Social closure

Social closure describes how groups monopolise opportunities such as jobs, positions or membership by restricting access to insiders. The criteria for access can be credentials, origin, language or citizenship. The concept goes back to Max Weber and shows that exclusion often results from others securing their own advantages.

Often confused with: spatial separation. Social closure concerns access to resources and positions, not where people live.




Othering

Othering is the process of constructing a group as fundamentally different from and inferior to one’s own. By defining “the others”, a group stabilises its own identity as “us”. Othering takes place in language, media, policies and everyday practices.

Often confused with: individual prejudice. Othering is a collective, discursive process, not merely a personal attitude.




Stigma

A stigma is an attribute or label that discredits a person and spoils their social identity. Once stigmatised, a person is no longer seen as a whole person but is reduced to that one feature. Stigma can lead to discrimination, and it also affects how people see themselves.

Often confused with: stereotype, a cognitive generalisation about a group, or with discrimination, the unequal treatment that may follow from stigma.

title: 1.4 Key terms and conceptual distinctions
text:
Analytical and normative concepts


Intersectionality

Intersectionality analyses how categories such as race, gender, class or disability overlap and together produce specific forms of disadvantage. A Black woman, for example, may face discrimination that neither Black men nor white women experience in the same way. The term was coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in legal studies.

Often confused with: an additive model in which several forms of discrimination are simply added up.




Recognition

Recognition means being affirmed as an equal and valued member of a community. It includes legal respect as a bearer of rights and social esteem for one’s abilities and way of life. Denied recognition is experienced as an injustice in its own right.

Often confused with: tolerance, which merely puts up with difference, or with redistribution, the material side of justice.




Citizenship

Citizenship is formal membership in a political community that grants rights and duties and allows claims on the state. Who holds citizenship and who is denied it is a central line of inclusion and exclusion. Formal citizenship does not guarantee that people are treated as full members in practice.

Often confused with: nationality, or with substantive belonging, which can be missing despite a passport.




Reasonable accommodation

Reasonable accommodation means necessary and appropriate adjustments in an individual case that enable a disabled person to exercise their rights on an equal basis with others. Examples are extra time in exams or an adapted workplace. Under the CRPD, denying reasonable accommodation counts as discrimination.

Often confused with: accessibility or universal design, which apply to everyone in advance rather than responding to one person’s needs.




Capability approach

The capability approach judges well-being by people’s real freedoms to do and be what they have reason to value. It asks not only which resources people have but what they can actually achieve with them. Developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum, it is widely used to assess social justice and development.

Often confused with: income or resource measures, or with skills and competencies in an educational sense.




Social cohesion

Social cohesion describes the degree of trust, shared belonging and cooperation that holds a community together across differences. Cohesive societies do not require sameness; they manage diversity and conflict without breaking apart. The term is common in European and national policy debates.

Often confused with: sameness or assimilation, or with social capital, the resources people gain from their networks.
